notes.h: Aim and stages of the grassland study
notes.b: An ecological investigation studies living things in their natural surroundings, and here the surroundings are a grassland habitat. The first job is to find out which organisms live there, because every later measurement is built on that list.
points: The aim is to find out which organisms live in a chosen grassland habitat (the place where a community of organisms lives), to collect and identify them, and so to build a species list. The surveys, abiotic measurements and feeding-relationship work are all based on that list.
Data gathered first-hand in the field, by your own counting, measuring and observing, are called primary data. Secondary data would come from books or other people’s work.
1. A preliminary visit to choose and map the study area (the mapping is done in the Surveys note).
2. Observe, collect and identify the organisms, which is the stage covered here.
3. A qualitative survey (which species are present, giving a species list) and a quantitative survey (how many of each) are carried out in the Surveys note.
4. Measure abiotic factors (non-living factors such as light and temperature) and relate them to the distribution and abundance of a species, as in the Abiotic factors note.
5. Work out feeding and symbiotic relationships (close partnerships between different species), as in the Biotic factors and relationships note.
6. Present the results and draw conclusions.
notes.tip: Remember that this stage is only about collecting and naming organisms. Quadrats, transects and the habitat map belong to the surveys stage, and measuring abiotic factors belongs to its own stage, so don’t answer a collection question with them.

notes.b: Before collecting anything you visit the site once to plan, because what you can find depends on the place, the time of year and the gear you bring.
points: On the preliminary visit, walk over the site and note its boundaries and main features: hedges, trees, paths, wet patches, slope and gate. These features create different microhabitats (small areas with their own conditions) that you will need to sample.
Get permission from the landowner, check access and hazards, and choose suitable dates, so that the work is legal and safe before anyone arrives with equipment.

Organisms change with the season, so collect over several visits if possible, for example late spring to early autumn, when most plants flower and most invertebrates (animals without backbones) are active.

Collecting equipment: pitfall traps (jars, trowel, flat stones or lids), pooter, sweep net, beating tray and stick, Tullgren funnel, collecting jars and labelled specimen tubes, and white trays on which small animals show up clearly.
Identification and recording equipment: hand lens, identification keys and field guides, camera or phone, notebook and pencil, and labels.
Protection and measuring equipment: gloves, tape measures, and quadrats (square frames used in the Surveys note).

notes.b: When you compare two areas or two times, the comparison is only fair if the collecting effort is the same each time. That means deciding what you change, what you measure and what you keep constant.
points: The independent variable (the one you choose to change) is the area or time sampled.
The dependent variable (the one you measure) is the kinds and numbers of organisms caught.
The controlled variables (kept the same) are the type and number of traps, the trapping time, the number of sweeps, the time of day and the weather, so that the collections are a fair comparison.
No true control is possible in a field study, because the conditions in the field can’t be held constant. This is why you control as many variables as you can and repeat the collection.
notes.tip: If asked for the variables in a collecting investigation, state independent, dependent and controlled variables separately, and say that a true control isn’t possible in the field.

notes.b: Not every organism can or should be caught. Large, fast or delicate organisms are studied by looking, and animals that hide are detected from the traces they leave.
points: Direct observation (looking at the organism itself) is used for organisms that are large, fast or that should not be caught, such as birds, rabbits, foxes and butterflies, and for all plants, which are identified where they grow and not dug up.
Use binoculars for birds and mammals at a distance, and a hand lens (about ×10) for small features such as the hairs or veins of a leaf.
Indirect signs show animals that are rarely seen: droppings, tracks in mud, burrows, nests, feathers, molehills and wormcasts.
Feeding signs are indirect signs too: nibbled leaves, holes in leaves made by slugs or caterpillars, and broken snail shells beside a stone used by a song thrush.

Record each observation at once, so nothing is forgotten: the organism (or ‘unknown species A’ with a sketch or photograph until it is identified) and where it was found (its microhabitat, for example under a stone or on a dandelion leaf).
Also record the time, the weather and what the organism was doing, such as feeding on what.
Photographs record organisms without removing them and can be checked later against keys, so record the location and date with each image.
notes.tip: Plants are identified where they grow, not pulled up. Mammals in grassland are usually recorded by observation and signs rather than trapped.

notes.h: Collecting ground animals: the pitfall trap
notes.b: Many grassland invertebrates (animals without backbones) walk over the soil surface and are hard to spot. A pitfall trap catches them as they travel, with no effort from the collector.
points: A pitfall trap is a jar or plastic cup sunk into a hole in the ground so that its rim is exactly level with the soil surface. Animals walking across the ground fall in and can’t climb the smooth sides.
A flat stone or lid raised on small stones covers the trap, which keeps out rain and stops birds and other predators taking the catch. Bait, such as a small piece of meat or fruit, can be added.
Pitfall traps catch ground-dwelling (crawling) invertebrates: ground beetles, spiders, woodlice, slugs, ants and millipedes.
Check traps at least every 24 hours, ideally early morning, because predators such as ground beetles and spiders will eat the other animals in the trap.
Remove all traps at the end of the study so that no animal is trapped later.
Diagram: a pitfall trap in section: jar in the soil with rim level with the surface, raised flat stone cover on small supports, bait, and animals inside. Label soil surface, jar, cover, bait.
notes.tip: Draw the rim level with the ground, not sticking up, because a raised rim stops animals falling in. For precautions, give checking every 24 hours and removing the traps afterwards.

notes.h: Collecting soil animals: the Tullgren funnel
notes.b: Tiny animals living in soil and leaf litter (the layer of dead leaves on the ground) are too small to pick out by hand. A Tullgren funnel gets them to leave the sample by themselves.
points: A Tullgren funnel extracts small animals from a sample of soil or leaf litter.
The sample sits on a wire mesh (gauze) in a funnel under a lamp, a light bulb about 10–20 cm above it.

The heat and light dry the sample from the top, so the animals move down away from the heat, light and dryness, through the mesh and into a collecting beaker below. The lamp drives the animals away; it does not attract them.
The beaker holds damp tissue paper to keep the animals alive, or ethanol if they are to be preserved for identification. Leave the funnel for several hours to a day.
A Tullgren funnel catches mites, springtails, small beetles and their larvae, and small worms.
The mesh must be fine enough to hold back the soil, and too hot a lamp kills the animals before they leave.

Diagram: a Tullgren funnel: lamp, soil or leaf-litter sample, wire gauze, funnel, collecting beaker with damp tissue (or ethanol), and an arrow showing animals moving down away from the heat and light.
notes.tip: Say the animals move down away from the lamp’s heat, light and drying. Never say the lamp attracts them.

notes.b: Earthworms and mammals need their own methods, because earthworms burrow too deeply for pitfall traps and mammals need careful, humane handling.
points: Earthworms are collected by digging a measured block of soil and sorting it by hand on a white tray, or by watering a marked area with a mustard-powder solution, which irritates them so that they come to the surface.
Rinse earthworms in clean water at once.
A small-mammal trap is a baited box with dry bedding and food inside. The door closes behind the animal, which is unharmed.
Small-mammal traps are used only under teacher supervision. Check them at least every few hours and release the animal where it was caught.
Some mammal species are protected by law, so trapping may need a licence. Mammals in grassland are more often recorded by observation and signs, because trapping them is restricted.

notes.h: Collecting animals on plants: sweep net and beating tray
notes.b: Many invertebrates live on stems and leaves rather than on the ground. Two methods knock them off the plants so they can be counted.
points: A sweep net is a strong net with a fine cloth bag on a stout frame and handle. Sweep it quickly through long grass and low plants in a series of side-to-side arcs while walking slowly, so that animals on the plants are knocked into the bag.
After sweeping, fold the bag over to close it, then empty it onto a white tray or into a jar.
A sweep net catches grasshoppers, aphids, flies, beetles, spiders, caterpillars and leafhoppers.
Use a fixed number of sweeps (for example ten) in each area so that catches can be compared.
A sweep net doesn’t work in wet grass, which soaks the bag and damages the animals.
A beating tray is a white sheet or tray (or an upturned umbrella) held under a branch of a hedge, shrub or tree at the grassland edge. The branch is struck sharply with a stick a set number of times.

Animals living on the branch fall onto the tray, where they are easy to see against the white. A beating tray catches caterpillars, beetles, spiders, ladybirds and shield bugs, which are then collected with a pooter.

notes.b: Small, fast animals are hard to pick up without crushing them. A pooter lets you suck them gently into a container.
points: A pooter is a clear container (jar or tube) closed by a stopper through which two tubes pass.
The user places the end of the long inlet tube next to a small animal and sucks on the mouthpiece tube. The animal is drawn up the inlet tube into the container.
A piece of fine gauze (muslin) over the inner end of the mouthpiece tube stops the animal or debris being sucked into the user’s mouth.
A pooter is used for small, fast-moving animals (small insects, spiders, springtails) from a beating tray, sweep net, the ground or bark.
Empty it often, because animals inside can harm each other.
Diagram: a pooter: container, stopper, inlet tube, mouthpiece tube, gauze over the inner end of the mouthpiece tube, arrows for the air flow and the animal entering.
notes.tip: The gauze goes on the mouthpiece tube, not the inlet tube. Students often draw it on the wrong tube.

notes.h: Collecting flying insects: butterfly net and light trap
notes.b: Flying insects escape from ground traps and sweep nets, so they need methods of their own. One works by day with a net and one by night with a lamp.
points: A butterfly net, a light, fine-meshed net on a long handle, catches flying insects such as butterflies and bees. Hold the net closed with a twist of the bag and release the insect after identification.
Bees and wasps can sting, so many are identified by observation instead of being caught.
A light trap (moth trap) is a bright lamp, often ultraviolet, above a box with egg trays inside, left on overnight.

Night-flying insects, mainly moths, are attracted to the light, fall into the box and settle in the trays. They are identified and released next morning, away from birds, which would otherwise eat them.

notes.b: Once animals are caught, they must be kept alive, named and recorded quickly, because the record is the data the whole investigation depends on.
points: Place animals in labelled jars or specimen tubes with a little vegetation, keep them cool and shaded, and identify them as soon as possible on a white tray with a hand lens.
Record for each catch the name (or ‘species A’), the number caught, the method and place of capture, and the date and time. These are the raw primary data used in the Surveys note.
Return every animal to the place where it was caught, after identification.
Collect plants only when they are common and can’t be identified where they grow, taking a single leaf or flower rather than the whole plant.
notes.tip: Animals are returned to where they were caught, and plants are identified where they grow rather than collected.

notes.b: Once you have an organism, you need its name. An identification key gets you there by asking a short series of questions about what you can see.
points: An identification key is a tool for naming an unknown organism by working through a series of questions or statements about its visible features.
A dichotomous key (‘dichotomous’ means dividing in two) gives a pair of contrasting statements at each step, called a couplet.
The user chooses the statement that fits the organism, and follows the number or name it leads to, until a name is reached.

Good keys use features that are easy to see and don’t vary between individuals or with age or season: number of legs, number of body parts, wings present or absent, shell present or absent, leaf shape and arrangement, flower colour and number of petals.
Good keys avoid size, which varies with age, and vague words such as ‘large’, because two users might judge them differently.
notes.tip: Exams ask what could help identify organisms (answer: a key) and ask you to use or make a simple key, so practise both.

notes.h: A worked key and how to make one
notes.b: Here is a key to five grassland invertebrates, written as numbered couplets. Work through it with an animal in mind, then see how such a key is built.
points: 1. Legs present: go to 2. No legs: go to 4.
2. Three pairs of legs (6 legs) and body in three parts (head, thorax, abdomen): insect (for example a ground beetle). More than 6 legs: go to 3.
3. Four pairs of legs (8 legs) and body in two parts: spider. Seven pairs of legs (14 legs) and body flattened and covered with overlapping plates: woodlouse.
4. Body made of many ring-like segments: earthworm. Body not segmented, soft and slimy: go to 5.
5. Shell present: snail. No shell: slug. Using the key: an animal with 14 legs goes 1, then 2, then 3, then woodlouse.
To make a key, list the organisms, then choose a feature that splits them into two groups.
Keep splitting each group with a new feature until each organism stands alone, then check the key by keying out each organism in turn to see that it reaches the right name.
A tree diagram (branching chart) of the same splits is another way to show a key.
notes.tip: Follow the key one couplet at a time and write the route you took, such as 1, 2, 3, woodlouse, so the examiner can see your reasoning.

notes.h: Other identification aids and naming organisms
notes.b: Keys are not the only help. Several other aids check or speed up an identification, and you still need a plan for organisms you can’t name.
points: Illustrated field guides and identification charts (for example of wild flowers, grasses, insects and birds) show pictures to compare with your specimen. You can also compare it with labelled specimens or photographs, or ask an expert such as a teacher or naturalist.
Image-recognition apps on a phone are an aid, but their suggestions must be checked against a key or guide, because they are often wrong for small invertebrates.
A hand lens or a stereo (dissecting) microscope shows small features that decide between similar species.

Identify each organism to species if possible. Where that isn’t possible, name the group (for example ‘a ground beetle’) and give it a code (species A, B …) used consistently throughout the study, so that it can still be counted in the surveys.

notes.h: Typical organisms of an Irish grassland
notes.b: Knowing what to expect makes identification quicker. These are the plants and animals typically found in an Irish grassland.
points: Typical plants: grasses (for example perennial ryegrass in pasture), daisy, dandelion, creeping buttercup, white clover, ribwort plantain and, in damp patches, rushes.
Daisy and dandelion grow as flat rosettes of leaves close to the ground, which helps them survive mowing and grazing.

Typical invertebrates: earthworms, slugs, snails, ground beetles, spiders, woodlice (in damp places under stones or logs), ants, aphids, grasshoppers, ladybirds, caterpillars, butterflies and bumblebees.
Typical vertebrates (animals with backbones): rabbits, the Irish hare, foxes, badgers, hedgehogs, wood mice, pygmy shrews, and birds such as the song thrush, blackbird and kestrel.

notes.h: How methods change in other habitats
notes.b: The methods above suit grassland. In other habitats the organisms and conditions differ, so you choose different methods to match.
points: Woodland: beating trays under branches and pitfall traps in the leaf litter are the main methods. Leaf-litter samples go in a Tullgren funnel, trees are identified by leaf, bark and fruit, and the layers (canopy, shrub, herb and ground layers) are recorded separately.

Rocky shore: animals are mostly collected by hand from under seaweed, in rock pools and under stones (turned back the right way up), or simply counted where they are, as many are attached (barnacles, limpets, mussels). Seaweeds are identified with a key.
Rocky shore work is done at low tide, ideally a spring low tide. Check tide tables first, and start at the lowest point as the tide goes out.
Freshwater (stream or pond): a pond net is swept through the water and vegetation.
In a stream, kick sampling is used: the net is held on the bed just downstream while the stones upstream are disturbed with the feet for a fixed time, so that animals are washed into the net.
The catch from kick sampling is emptied into a white tray of water and identified, for example mayfly, stonefly and caddis fly larvae, freshwater shrimps, snails and leeches.
A plankton net (very fine mesh) is towed slowly through the water to collect microscopic organisms.
Freshwater animals are kept in water from the same habitat and returned quickly.
notes.tip: If asked how methods change for a different habitat, name the habitat, the method (such as kick sampling in a stream) and why it suits that habitat.

notes.b: Fieldwork takes you away from the classroom, so you must plan for risks on land and near water.
points: Work in groups, never alone, and tell someone where you are going. Wear suitable clothes and footwear for the weather.
Take care near livestock, electric fences, nettles and brambles. Wear gloves when handling soil, leaf litter and traps, cover cuts, and wash hands before eating.
Check for ticks after working in long grass, because ticks can carry the bacterium that causes Lyme disease.
Be aware of anyone with an allergy to bee or wasp stings.
Near water, never work alone, and check the depth and the current before entering a stream.
At the shore, know the tide times, watch for incoming tides and take care on wet, slippery rocks covered with seaweed.
Cover cuts and wash hands after contact with fresh water, which can carry the bacteria that cause leptospirosis (Weil’s disease), spread in the urine of rats.
notes.tip: A precaution question wants a specific action matched to the hazard, such as checking for ticks after long grass or checking the tide times at the shore.

notes.b: Collecting can damage the habitat you are studying. A code of conduct protects the habitat and its organisms.
points: Get permission from the landowner, close gates, and keep disturbance and trampling to a minimum.
Replace stones and logs the way they were found, because animals beneath them depend on the damp, dark conditions.
Handle animals gently and return them to where they were caught.
Don’t pick or uproot plants unnecessarily, and never collect protected or rare species.
Remove all traps and litter at the end of the study.
notes.tip: Expect questions on the ethical code of conduct for fieldwork, so give specific actions such as returning animals and replacing stones.

notes.b: A species list from one afternoon is never complete. Each method, and each visit, has built-in limits that you should recognise and reduce.
points: Each collection method catches only some kinds of organism: pitfall traps catch only animals that walk on the ground, and sweep nets only animals on tall plants. Several methods must be used to build a complete species list.
Catches depend on the weather, the time of day and the season. Many animals are nocturnal or are active only in warm, dry or damp conditions, so one visit misses many species.
Repeat collections on several days and at different times, under similar conditions when comparing areas.
Animals in traps may escape or be eaten by others before they are counted, so check traps often. Birds may take the catch from uncovered traps.
Misidentification, especially of small invertebrates and of grasses that are not in flower, is a source of error. Check identifications with a second key or guide, or with the teacher.
Disturbance by the collectors (trampling, noise) changes animals’ behaviour and damages the habitat.
notes.tip: For a limitation, link the method to the organisms it misses, then give the improvement, such as using several methods or repeating the collection.

keyTerms.definition: Data gathered first-hand by the student in the field, such as the species and numbers caught in a study.
Evidence that an animal is present without seeing it, such as droppings, tracks, burrows, nests, feathers and feeding signs.
A jar sunk into the soil with its rim level with the surface, covered to keep out rain and predators, to catch ground-dwelling animals that walk into it.
Apparatus in which a lamp dries a soil or leaf-litter sample so that small animals move down and fall through a mesh into a collecting beaker.
A container with an inlet tube and a mouthpiece tube, used to suck small animals into the container; gauze over the inner end of the mouthpiece tube stops them entering the mouth.
A strong net with a fine cloth bag, swept through grass and low plants to knock animals on the plants into the bag.
A white tray held under a branch that is struck with a stick, so that animals living on the branch fall onto the tray.
A bright lamp above a box that attracts night-flying insects, mainly moths, which fall into the box and settle in egg trays.
A tool for naming an unknown organism by working through a series of questions about its visible features.
An identification key in which each step gives a pair of contrasting statements, one of which fits the organism.
The pair of contrasting statements given at one step of a dichotomous key.
A label such as species A used consistently for an organism that cannot be identified to species, so that it can still be counted.

questions.prompt: Name a piece of apparatus used to collect (i) animals that crawl on the ground and (ii) small insects from a beating tray, and give one precaution taken when using each.
questions.model: (i) A pitfall trap: a jar sunk into the soil so that its rim is level with the surface, covered with a flat stone or lid raised on small stones. Precaution: check it at least every 24 hours, so that predators such as ground beetles and spiders do not eat the other animals in the trap; remove all traps at the end of the study. (ii) A pooter: a container with an inlet tube and a mouthpiece tube. Precaution: the gauze over the inner end of the mouthpiece tube stops the animal or debris being sucked into the mouth, and the container should be emptied often because animals inside can harm each other.

questions.prompt: Describe how a Tullgren funnel is used to collect animals from leaf litter, and explain why the animals move into the collecting vessel.
questions.model: Put the leaf-litter sample on a wire mesh (gauze) in a funnel. Place a lamp about 10–20 cm above the sample. Put a collecting beaker under the funnel, with damp tissue paper in it (or ethanol if the animals are to be preserved). Leave for several hours to a day. The heat and light from the lamp dry the sample from the top, so the animals move down away from the heat, light and dryness. They fall through the mesh into the beaker. The lamp drives the animals away from it; it does not attract them. The damp tissue keeps the animals alive in the beaker.

questions.prompt: Explain what a dichotomous key is. Construct a key to separate a spider, a woodlouse, an insect and a slug, and give two other ways an ecologist might identify an organism found in a grassland.
questions.model: A dichotomous key is an identification tool that gives a pair of contrasting statements at each step (a couplet); the user chooses the statement that fits the organism and follows the number it leads to until a name is reached. Key: 1. Legs present → go to 2. No legs → slug. 2. Six legs (three pairs) → insect. More than six legs → go to 3. 3. Eight legs (four pairs) → spider. Fourteen legs (seven pairs) → woodlouse. The key uses only the number of legs, not size or colour. Two other ways to identify the organism: use an illustrated field guide or identification chart; compare it with labelled specimens or photographs, or ask an expert such as a teacher or naturalist.
